quote_orig: וְעַתָּ֡ה שְׁנֵֽי־בָנֶ֩יךָ֩ הַנּוֹלָדִ֨ים לְךָ֜ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֗יִם עַד־בֹּאִ֥י אֵלֶ֛יךָ מִצְרַ֖יְמָה לִי־הֵ֑ם אֶפְרַ֙יִם֙ וּמְנַשֶּׁ֔ה כִּרְאוּבֵ֥ן וְשִׁמְע֖וֹן יִֽהְיוּ־לִֽי׃ וּמוֹלַדְתְּךָ֛ אֲשֶׁר־הוֹלַ֥דְתָּ אַחֲרֵיהֶ֖ם לְךָ֣ יִהְי֑וּ עַ֣ל שֵׁ֧ם אֲחֵיהֶ֛ם יִקָּרְא֖וּ בְּנַחֲלָתָֽם׃
quote_en: And now thy two sons, who were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine. And thy issue, that thou begettest after them, shall be thine; they shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.
licence_note: Hebrew: Sefaria version "Miqra according to the Masorah", CC-BY-SA. English: JPS 1917, Public Domain (Sefaria version metadata).
keys: even as Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine
they shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance
what_it_shows: In Jacob's words, Joseph's two sons born in Egypt "shall be mine" as Reuben and Simeon are, and any later children of Joseph "shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance". The text speaks of counting them as sons and of their name and inheritance; it does not use a word for adoption.
context: Jacob, dying in Egypt, sees Joseph's sons (48:1–11) and declares their status before blessing them (48:15–20). The Bava Batra 123a Gemara (P08) quotes 48:22, which follows in the same chapter, about Jacob giving Joseph one portion above his brothers.
limits: The verse gives no legal formula; it is Jacob's declaration in a deathbed setting. How "shall be called ... in their inheritance" should be read is disputed: Rashi (P05) says the later-born are not counted among Jacob's sons and have no tribal name for inheritance; Rashbam (P06, on 48:6) says they are family houses (בתי אבות), not tribes; Ramban (P07) reads 48:6 as confirming a double share for the two sons. Sforno (48:5, Munk CC-BY) reads "mine" as a gift of these two sons "together with you", not a legal transfer (see the summary).

to: name of their brethren in their inheritance.

quote_en: And now thy two sons which were born to thee in the land of Mizraim, before my coming to thee into Mizraim, are mine; Ephraim and Menashe shall be as Reuben and Shimeon before me. And the children whom thou mayest beget after them, who shall be thine, after the name of their brethren they shall be called in their inheritance.

what_it_shows: The Aramaic translation renders "shall be mine" as "shall be before me" (קֳדָמָי), like Reuben and Simeon, and renders 48:6 as "they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance" (בְּאַחֲסַנְתְּהוֹן). It is a translation of the verse and adds no legal reasoning.
context: Onkelos is the standard Babylonian Aramaic translation of the Torah (Sefaria's note on Pseudo-Jonathan calls it "the eastern Babylonian Targum Onkelos"). Radak on 48:6 (Munk CC-BY) says that the rendering of "ומולדתך" as "you will beget" (future) is Onkelos's reading.
limits: It is a translation, so it does not explain the basis of the status. Its verb in 48:5 is "before me", not "mine". Radak (48:5) says Jacob means only these two, not all of Joseph's sons. Onkelos on 50:23 (Machir's children, P11) uses a root meaning "raise", which points to nurture rather than tribe transfer.

And thy children whom thou mayest beget after them shall be thine; by the name of their brethren shall they be called in their inheritance.

what_it_shows: Pseudo-Jonathan renders "mine" in 48:5 with "are reckoned to me" (מִתְחַשְׁבִין לִי), the same idea as Rashi's "בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן" ("in the reckoning"), and renders 48:6 as "shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance". It does not describe a legal procedure.
context: Pseudo-Jonathan is an expansive Palestinian Targum. Sefaria's description says its date is disputed: it "cannot have been completed before the Arab conquest as it refers to Mohammad's wife Fatima, but might have been initially composed in the 4th Century CE. However, some scholars date it in the 14th Century."
limits: The late and disputed date (Sefaria's own note) means it is not early evidence for what the verse meant. The English is Etheridge's 1862 translation. Pseudo-Jonathan is a mixture of translation and aggadic material, so it is not a legal text.

quote_orig: לי הם. בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן שְׁאָר בָּנַי הֵם, לִטֹּל חֵלֶק בָּאָרֶץ אִישׁ כְּנֶגְדּוֹ
quote_en: לי הם THEY SHALL BE MINE — they shall be counted amongst my other sons, to receive a portion in the Land each for himself (i.e. each to have his own territory exactly as each of my other sons has).

what_it_shows: Rashi says "לי הם" ("they are mine") means that Ephraim and Manasseh are "counted in the reckoning of my other sons", so that each receives a land portion exactly as each of Jacob's other sons does. He speaks of counting and of equal land shares; he does not say "adoption" and does not say a double share.
context: Rashi's first sentence glosses "before I came to you" (עַד בֹּאִי אֵלֶיךָ) as "that they were born from the time you left me until I came to you". The "לי הם" gloss is his answer to the Hebrew "mine".
limits: Rashi does not say adoption or a double share here. On 48:6 (P05) he says the later-born are not counted among Jacob's sons, so the "counting" is restricted to these two. Rashi's gloss on 1 Chr 5:1 (P10) limits the birthright to a double share and not to the kingship or the genealogical firstborn.

Numbers 26:55), and of appointing princes to the various tribes and of assigning banners to each of them.
licence_note: Rosenbaum & Silbermann 1929–34 (Hebrew and English): Public Domain (Sefaria version metadata). The Sefaria English omits the first sentence of the Hebrew; that sentence is only in the Hebrew.

what_it_shows: Rashi says that any later children of Joseph would not be counted among Jacob's sons but would be included within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, with no tribal name for inheritance. Although the land was divided by head, only Joseph's two sons were called "tribes" (for the lots, the princes and the banners).
context: Rashi's first sentence (Hebrew only on Sefaria; team translation): "If you beget more, they will not be counted in my sons' number, but will be included among the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, and will have no name among the tribes with regard to inheritance." The English quoted is Rosenbaum's.
limits: This is a direct limit on the thesis. Rashi holds the later-born are not tribes and have no tribal name for inheritance, so tribe was not handed on to Joseph's descendants. Ramban (P07) summarises Rashi as making Joseph's firstborn status "only for honor" and rejects that reading. Rashbam (P06, 48:6) also denies tribal status to the later-born.

what_it_shows: Rashbam reads 48:5 as Jacob's power, given the land of Canaan, to make Joseph firstborn with a double share ("two tribes' portion"), so that Joseph's two sons take the place of Reuben and Simeon in the division of the land.
context: This is Rashbam's own reading, not the text. The Hebrew "הרי ברשותי" ("it is in my power") is his wording.
limits: Rashbam on 48:6 (daat, Hebrew; Munk CC-BY) says the later-born "will not be tribes but only houses of fathers (בתי אבות)", that is, heads of family groups within Ephraim or Manasseh. So he gives the double share to the two sons and denies tribal status to their later children. Rashbam's claim is the commentator's, not the Torah's.

what_it_shows: Ramban holds that Jacob's grant of the firstborn right to Joseph was for inheritance: Joseph and his sons took a double share as the firstborn does, and "in their inheritance" means this. He rejects Rashi's reading that the firstborn status was only the name "tribe" (Ramban calls this reading "only for honor"), and cites Bava Batra 123a.
context: Ramban's comment on 48:6 quotes Rashi's words first (the English quotes Rashi in Chavel's translation), then argues against them. The Hebrew quoted is his own text.
limits: Ramban is a medieval commentator, not the text. He cites Horayot 6b, which says (Chavel English, CC-BY): "I have likened Ephraim and Menasheh to Reuben and Simeon with respect to the matter of inheritance, but not with respect to other matters" (P09). That is a limit on parity: inheritance only. Ramban also argues from this that the land was not divided per head, which the verse does not say.

own_translation_en: The verse says "birthright" (בכורה) about Joseph, and it says "birthright" about the later generations. Just as the birthright said of Joseph is a double portion ("two-fold as for one"), so the birthright said of the later generations is a double portion ("two-fold as for one").
licence_note: Hebrew/Aramaic: Sefaria "William Davidson Edition - Vocalized Aramaic", CC-BY-NC (the Vilna text is public domain, but this copy is CC-BY-NC; Wikisource copy not retrieved). English: none quoted (William Davidson English is CC-BY-NC); own translation supplied.
keys: נֶאֶמְרָה
פִּי שְׁנַיִם כְּאֶחָד
what_it_shows: The Gemara says the Torah uses "birthright" both of Joseph and of the later generations, and that the birthright is a double portion. So, by the Talmud's own rule, the birthright Jacob gave to Joseph's sons means a double share in the inheritance. The Gemara's proof texts are I Chr 5:1–2 (for Joseph) and Deut 21:17 (for the later generations; per the William Davidson English, not quoted).
context: In the Gemara's discussion of why Jacob took the birthright from Reuben and gave it to Joseph (Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani), the Gemara first quotes I Chr 5:1 and then the rule above; then, in a sharp exchange with Rav Pappa, Abaye quotes Gen 48:5 ("Ephraim and Manasseh shall be like Reuben and Simeon to me").
limits: The same page quotes I Chr 5:1 that the birthright was given to Joseph's sons "yet not so that he was to be reckoned in the genealogy as firstborn" (לְהִתְיַחֵשׂ לַבְּכֹרָה), which separates the double share from the genealogical firstborn status (see P10). The Gemara answers Rabbi Chelbo's question with a parable of a householder who raised an orphan, who later enriched him; the analogy presents the transfer as a return for kindness, not as a legal formula. Horayot 6b (P09) limits the parity to inheritance. Rashbam (A2-W16, Hebrew Vilna, PD) on the same words: "ולא להתיחש על הבכורה - לא שיקרא בכור ניתנה לו בכורה דלעולם ראובן קרי בכור ישראל אלא ליטול שני חלקים כבכור" ("the birthright was given, but Reuben is still called firstborn of Israel; it is only to take two portions as firstborn"). Rabbeinu Gershom (A2-W17, Hebrew Vilna, PD): the double share is "ולא בכל הנכסים" ("and not in all possessions"), i.e. only in the land portion.

own_translation_en: Abaye said: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be like Reuben and Simeon to me" (Gen 48:5). Rava said: But it is written, "they shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance" (Gen 48:6). They were compared (equated) to them for inheritance, and not for another matter! The Gemara objects that they are separate tribes for the banners, and answers that the banner arrangement was "in order to honor" the banners ("as their inheritance, so their encampment").

וְלֹא לְדָבָר אַחֵר
what_it_shows: In the Gemara, Abaye counts Ephraim and Manasseh as two tribes from Gen 48:5. Rava replies from Gen 48:6 that they were made equal to Reuben and Simeon "for inheritance and not for another matter". So the Talmud limits the tribal parity to inheritance.
context: The discussion is about whether there are twelve tribes when Levi, which has no inherited land, is not counted (a tribe is a "congregation" only if it has an ancestral possession). Abaye and Rava debate Ephraim and Manasseh.
limits: Rava's own ruling is the limit: parity "for inheritance and not for another matter". The Gemara objects that Ephraim and Manasseh are also separate for the banners and for the princes; it answers that the banners were arranged "in order to honor" the tribes (כָּבוֹד לַדְּגָלִים) and the princes likewise (Hebrew: "כְּנַחֲלָתָן כָּךְ חֲנִיָּיתָן, כְּדֵי לְחַלֵּק כָּבוֹד לַדְּגָלִים"). So the Gemara treats the tribal status as inheritance-only. Rashi on Horayot 6b:3:1 (A2-W18, Hebrew Vilna, PD) supports the parity: "דבתרי שבטים חשיב להו כראובן ושמעון" ("he counts them as two tribes, like Reuben and Simeon").

quote_en: And the sons of Reuben the first-born of Israel—for he was the first-born; but, forasmuch as he defiled his father’s couch, his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, yet not so that he was to be reckoned in the genealogy as first-born. For Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came he that is the prince; but the birthright was Joseph’s—
licence_note: Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah, CC-BY-SA. English: JPS 1917, Public Domain. Rashi (on Sefaria): Hebrew "Sefaria vocalized edition", licence unknown; English Judaica Press (Rosenberg), CC-BY.
keys: yet not so that he was to be reckoned in the genealogy as first-born
but the birthright was Joseph’s
what_it_shows: The Chronicler says that Reuben's birthright, forfeited through his sin, "was given unto the sons of Joseph", yet "not so that he was to be reckoned in the genealogy as first-born". The verse separates the birthright (inheritance) from genealogical reckoning, and Judah leads.
context: The genealogy of Israel in 1 Chr 5 begins with Reuben, then gives the birthright to Joseph's sons and the kingship to Judah. Rashi glosses the verse on 5:1 (Hebrew: Sefaria "vocalized edition", licence listed as unknown; English: Judaica Press, CC-BY).
limits: This verse is a direct limit: the birthright went to Joseph's sons, but not the genealogical firstborn status. Rashi on 5:1 (Hebrew: "וְלֹא לְהִתְיַחֵשׂ לַבְּכֹרָה – חֵלֶק בְּכוֹרוֹת וְלֹא בְּכוֹר") explains that Joseph's sons took a double portion but not the firstborn position; the Judaica Press English: "[i.e., the sons of Joseph were not meant] to take the share of the kingship, but only the birthright". Ramban (P07) argues the double share was real inheritance.

quote_en: And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he, and his father’s house; and Joseph lived a hundred and ten years. And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation; the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were born upon Joseph’s knees.

keys: were born upon Joseph’s knees
the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh
what_it_shows: The verse says that Machir's children, Machir being a son of Manasseh (so Joseph's grandson), "were born upon Joseph's knees". Rashi glosses it: "as the Targum gives it: He brought them up upon his knees". The phrase is about being raised in Joseph's household; the verse keeps them in Machir's line.
context: Gen 50:23 is near the end of the Joseph narrative (Joseph sees Ephraim's children of the third generation; 50:26 records his death). Onkelos (PD Aramaic) reads "born, and raised by Joseph" (אִתְיְלִידוּ וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵף) with a root meaning "to raise". Rashi glosses the same "knees" phrase at Gen 30:3 (P12).
limits: Rashi (PD) reads "on the knees" as nurture ("he brought them up") and not as legal reckoning. The verse gives Machir son of Manasseh as their line; it does not say the children took Joseph's or Ephraim's tribe, name or inheritance. This passage shows a fostering idiom, not a tribe transfer.

quote_en: And she said: ‘Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; that she may bear upon my knees, and I also may be builded up through her.’
licence_note: Hebrew: Miqra, CC-BY-SA. JPS 1917: Public Domain. Rashi: Public Domain (Rosenbaum & Silbermann). Genesis Rabbah English: Sefaria Midrash Rabbah 2022, CC-BY.
keys: that she may bear upon my knees
I also may be builded up through her
what_it_shows: Rachel says that Bilhah will bear "upon my knees" and that "I also may be builded up through her". Rashi (PD): "as the Targum takes it: she will bear children and I will rear them". Genesis Rabbah 71:7 (CC-BY): "just as that one was built through her rival wife, this one too was built through her rival wife", comparing Sarah and Hagar; Rachel then names Bilhah's son Dan.
context: The verse is in the Rachel–Leah rivalry (Gen 30:1–6). Rashi on "upon my knees" cites Onkelos (PD Aramaic: "וַאֲנָא אֱרַבֵּי וְאֶתְבְּנֵי", "I shall be raised and built up"). The "built through" idiom is the common reading in Rashi and the Midrash.
limits: The verse and both commentaries describe a mother having and rearing children through a handmaid. They do not say what happens to the child's tribe, name or inheritance; the passage does not address that. The Midrash is aggadic, and Rashi reads the phrase as rearing. So this supports a maternal fiction of "as if born to me", not a legal transfer of tribe.

what_it_shows: This midrash lists the places where Ephraim is placed before Manasseh: birth-listing, lineage, inheritance (quoted here), banners, princes, judges, kings and blessing. It treats both as tribes and as lineages of Joseph. It does not mention adoption or legal sonship.

quote_en: 170. If his wife bear sons to a man, or his maid-servant have borne sons, and the father while still living says to the children whom his maid-servant has borne: "My sons," and he count them with the sons of his wife; if then the father die, then the sons of the wife and of the maid-servant shall divide the paternal property in common. The son of the wife is to partition and choose. 171. If, however, the father while still living did not say to the sons of the maid-servant: "My sons," and then the father dies, then the sons of the maid-servant shall not share with the sons of the wife, but the freedom of the maid and her sons shall be granted.
licence_note: The Avalon Project page (King 1910 translation) showed no licence line in the text read; the 1910 King translation is public domain by age (per the brief).
keys: My sons,
The son of the wife is to partition and choose.
what_it_shows: In the Babylonian code, if a father, while living, calls his maidservant's sons "my sons" and counts them with his wife's sons, all of them divide the paternal property (the wife's son partitions and chooses first). If he did not, the maidservant's sons get no share but are granted freedom. So acknowledgment by the father could give a child of a slave-woman an inheritance share.
context: Hammurabi's code (c. 1750 BCE) regulates the property of Mesopotamian households. It is a different legal world from Israel, and it is used here only to show how acknowledgment of sonship worked for inheritance.
limits: The code concerns inheritance of paternal property only. It says nothing about name, lineage, tribe, priesthood or royal succession. Acknowledgment has to happen in the father's lifetime, and without it the children get freedom and no share. The wife's son has priority in the partition. Only the English was read; the Akkadian was not read.

to: maid and her sons shall be granted.

quote_en: The sons of a man's sons are like his own sons. Whence do we learn (this)? From Jacob, because it is said, "Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine" (Gen. 48:5). Were they his sons? Were they not the sons of his son? But it teaches thee that the sons of a man's sons are as his own sons.
licence_note: Friedlander 1916 (English) and Sefaria Vocalized Edition (Hebrew): Public Domain (Sefaria version metadata).
keys: The sons of a man's sons are like his own sons
Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine
what_it_shows: This aggadic text uses Gen 48:5 to teach that a man's grandsons are 'like his own sons'; it adds a parallel from Laban (Gen 31:43) on daughters' sons. It reckons Jacob's grandsons as sons; it does not mention adoption, tribe or inheritance.
context: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 36:7, read on Sefaria in both Hebrew (vocalized, PD) and Friedlander's English (1916, PD). The surrounding chapter was not read.
limits: This is a grandson-as-son principle and does not describe an adoptee or a tribal or inheritance transfer. The same verse is used in Ketubot 72b:5 (Talmud), where it serves as a mnemonic and the Sefaria English (William Davidson, CC-BY-NC, not quoted) says it "teaches that grandchildren have the status of children"; Rashi there (A2-W19, Hebrew Vilna, PD): "אפרים ומנשה וגו' - בני בניו כבניו" ("Ephraim and Manasseh… grandsons are like sons"). That rule is about the case in Ketubot (cursing a husband's parents), not inheritance. Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer is a late aggadic text (date not checked).
from_: The sons of a man's sons are
to: man's sons are as his own sons.

what_it_shows: The midrash says Jacob "began making Joseph's sons tribes" (שְׁבָטִים) when he said "Ephraim and Manasseh, like Reuben and Simeon, shall be mine" (Gen 48:5). This is a rabbinic statement that Jacob's words made the two sons tribes.

quote_orig: כראובן ושמעון יהיו לי: לא אמר שיהיה יוסף הבכור כראובן, וגם אחר זה יעקב עצמו אמר ראובן בכורי אתה ולא אמר ליוסף שיהיה הוא הבכור. ע"כ נ"ל כי עד יעקב לא היה פי שנים נוהג, רק מאהבתו את יוסף נתן לו פי שנים, ואולי מזה נמשך אח"כ משפט פי שנים לבכור, ע"כ בד"ה כתוב (א' ה' א') נתנה בכורתו ליוסף, קורא למתנת פי שנים בכורה מפני שהבכור היה נוטל פי שנים, ואוהב גר ז"ל מוסיף כי גם ממה שאמר כראובן ושמעון יהיו לי משמע שלא היה פי שנים לראובן; ואם היה שכבר ניטלה הבכורה מראובן (כדעת בעל ד"ה) היה לו לפרש זה, ולפחות היה לו לומר כשמעון ולוי, לא כראובן ושמעון.
own_translation_en: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon": he did not say that Joseph would be the firstborn like Reuben. Afterwards Jacob himself said "Reuben, you are my firstborn" and did not say this of Joseph. So I think that until Jacob the double portion was not in force; out of his love for Joseph he gave him a double portion, and perhaps the law of the double portion for the firstborn arose from this. Chronicles therefore calls the gift of the double portion a "birthright", since the firstborn took a double portion. Shadal also cites a commentator he calls "Ohev Ger" that from "like Reuben and Simeon shall be mine" Reuben had no double portion; and if the birthright had been taken from Reuben, he should have said "like Simeon and Levi", not "like Reuben and Simeon".
licence_note: Sefaria 'Shadal 1st Edition': Public Domain. English: own translation (none quoted).
keys: לא אמר שיהיה יוסף הבכור כראובן
עד יעקב לא היה פי שנים נוהג
what_it_shows: Shadal argues that Gen 48:5 does not make Joseph the firstborn, and that the double portion was not in force before Jacob. On this view Jacob gave Joseph a double portion out of love, and the "birthright" wording in Chronicles names that gift.
context: Shadal's comment on 48:5 (19th century), read in Hebrew only (Sefaria, 1st edition). It is a commentary, not a text of the Torah.
limits: Shadal is a counter-view, and a late one. He denies the firstborn reading that Rashi, Ramban and the Talmud (Bava Batra 123a, P08) take for granted, and he treats the double portion as Jacob's gift, not a law already in force. His argument rests on the "birthright" wording in 1 Chr 5:1 and on his reading of 48:5 that Reuben kept the double portion.
